1.title: Tools, Capability Bloat and Progressive Discovery
1.text: Welcome to Module seven: Tools, Capability Bloat and Progressive Discovery. This module covers tools, capability bloat and progressive discovery. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. What capability bloat is and how it harms cost, accuracy and security. How to audit a tool and agent configuration. Progressive discovery: tool search, deferred loading, code execution with M C P (Model Context Protocol). Monolithic context versus progressive discovery: when each wins. Tool design for the agent-computer interface.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lumen Advisory Audits a Support Agent With 140 Tools
1.text: Our running case is Lumen Advisory. Lumen Advisory Audits a Support Agent With one hundred forty Tools. A client connected five M C P servers to one agent: ticketing, billing, C R M, wiki and monitoring. The agent now carries one hundred forty tool definitions, picks the wrong tool, answers slowly and costs more. It can also change billing plans and close accounts, though support staff only read tickets and draft replies.

1.title: Capability Bloat
1.text: Capability Bloat. Capability bloat equals more tools, permissions and context than the role needs.

1.title: Capability Bloat, continued
1.text: Capability Bloat, continued. The figure shows this: Capability bloat harms tokens and latency, accuracy through tool confusion, and security through excess privilege.

1.title: Capability Bloat, continued
1.text: Capability Bloat, continued. Tokens and latency. A multi-server setup (for example five common servers) can use about fifty-five thousand tokens of definitions before any work. Accuracy. Tool selection degrades beyond about thirty to fifty tools. Security. Every tool is attack surface: a successful injection can use any tool the agent holds. Cost and caching. Larger prefixes cost more and can be disturbed by changes. Maintenance. More descriptions to keep consistent. Audit questions. Which tools does this role actually need? Remove the rest (least privilege). Are descriptions distinct enough that two tools are not confused?

1.title: Capability Bloat, continued
1.text: Capability Bloat, continued. Can several fine-grained tools be merged into one well-designed tool? Which tools are used rarely: candidates for deferred loading? Does any tool allow destructive or irreversible actions without a gate? Exam tip: The first fix for excess capability is to remove tools the role does not need (least privilege). Logging or confirmation prompts are compensating controls, not removal of the privilege.

1.title: Progressive Discovery
1.text: Progressive Discovery. Instead of loading everything, expose capabilities on demand.

1.title: Progressive Discovery, continued
1.text: Progressive Discovery, continued. The figure shows this: Monolithic context loads every definition up front; progressive discovery lets the model search the catalog and load only the three to five tools it needs.

1.title: Progressive Discovery, continued
1.text: Progressive Discovery, continued. Tool search tool. How it works: Mark tools defer loading: true; the model searches the catalog (regex or B M twenty-five variant) and only matches load. Notes: All definitions are still sent in tools; at least one tool stays non-deferred; keep the three to five most used tools non-deferred; up to ten thousand tools; typically cuts definition tokens by over eighty-five percent. Custom search. How it works: Your own tool (embeddings) returns tool reference blocks. Notes: For semantic matching. M C P toolsets. How it works: Set defer loading in the mcp toolset default or per tool. Notes: Aggregating many servers.

1.title: Progressive Discovery, continued
1.text: Progressive Discovery, continued. Code execution with M C P. How it works: Present servers as a code A P I (application programming interface) in a file tree; the agent lists and reads only needed files, and filters data in code. Notes: Example reduction from about one hundred fifty thousand to two thousand tokens; needs a secure sandbox. Skills. How it works: Metadata always, instructions on trigger. Notes: For procedures. Use tool search when you have ten or more tools, definitions over ten thousand tokens, tool accuracy dropping, or many M C P servers (hundreds of tools). Standard calling is fine under about ten tools or when every tool is used on every request.

1.title: Progressive Discovery, continued
1.text: Progressive Discovery, continued. Naming: use consistent prefixes (github, slack ) and keywords in descriptions so one search finds a whole group; add a system-prompt line describing the categories. Caching: a deferred tool cannot carry cache control; deferred loading keeps the cached prefix stable. Code execution keeps intermediate data out of the model (a ten thousand-row sheet filtered to a few rows) and can tokenize sensitive values; its cost is the sandbox's operational and security overhead.

1.title: Monolithic versus progressive
1.text: Monolithic versus progressive. Fits. Monolithic context: Small, stable tool or knowledge sets; every item used each time. Progressive discovery: Large or growing catalogs; rare use. Pros. Monolithic context: Simple; cache-friendly; no search step. Progressive discovery: Fewer tokens; better selection; scales. Cons. Monolithic context: Bloat, confusion, cost at scale. Progressive discovery: Extra search step and latency; needs good names and descriptions.

1.title: Tool Design for the Agent-Computer Interface
1.text: Tool Design for the Agent-Computer Interface. Treat tool design like interface design: invest as much as in a human U I. Write descriptions like a docstring for a junior developer: purpose, parameters, examples, edge cases, boundaries from similar tools. Poka-yoke: make mistakes hard (for example, require absolute paths). Choose formats the model writes easily; avoid overhead such as counting lines. Return only what the next step needs; keep tool results compact and structured, with clear error messages. Test with many inputs, observe mistakes, iterate; one team spent more time on tools than on the prompt. Exam tip: Deferred tools are still sent in tools; deferral only keeps them out of the context until found. Exam tip: Use tool search from about ten tools or ten thousand tokens of definitions; under that, plain tool calling is simpler.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Bloat: About fifty-five thousand tokens for five servers; accuracy falls beyond thirty to fifty tools; more attack surface. First fix: Remove tools the role does not need. Tool search: Defer; regex or B M twenty-five; keep three to five loaded. Code execution with M C P: Code A P I in a file tree; filter in sandbox. Monolithic: Simple, cache-friendly, small stable sets. A C I: Docstring-quality descriptions, examples, poka-yoke, compact results.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A procurement agent can read purchase orders, draft supplier emails, approve payments and cancel contracts, but buyers only need it to read orders and draft emails. Which change best reduces risk? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Least privilege removes the unneeded capability; logs and dialogs only compensate for it.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. An agent connected to five M C P servers carries one hundred forty tools and often calls the wrong one. What should the architect try? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Deferred loading with search reduces definition tokens and selection confusion.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. For which situation is standard tool calling (without tool search) the better fit? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Few, always-used, small tools do not need discovery.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. An agent processes a ten thousand-row spreadsheet through tool calls and runs out of context. Which approach addresses the cause? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Keeping intermediate results out of the model saves tokens and errors.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Select two. Which two are valid statements about the tool search tool? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and E. Deferral controls what enters the context, not what is sent.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. What is the main trade-off of progressive discovery compared with a monolithic context? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Discovery trades a search step for lean context.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Which tool-design practice reduces misuse by the model? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Clear interfaces and poka-yoke design lower error rates.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: C. Question two: C. Question three: D. Question four: A. Question five: B and E. Question six: C. Question seven: C. In the next module, we continue the course.
